title: Front rack holds tutorial
summary: NH explains front rack holds, borrowed from Olympic weightlifting, which he has done for two years. They strengthen the front rack, thoracic extension, core and upper back statically, carrying over to front squats and pulls from the floor. He covers safety (inside the rack, no walkout, minimal knee bend), progression from front-squat weight, timing (short holds) and programming as a superset secondary lift.

claims.claim: NH borrows techniques from sports he respects, like Olympic weightlifting, to make his training more interesting; he has done front rack holds for two years.
If you don't front squat, front rack holds are useless: the technical mastery needed isn't worth it since the benefits mostly carry over to front squats.
For about 80% of people, front squats are limited not by the legs but by thoracic extension, upper-back strength and elbow/wrist flexibility.
Front squats fail by the thoracic spine rounding forward and the bar dumping; unlike a back squat you can't good-morning it up. NH has never seen anyone fail with a perfect rack going straight down.
Carryover is limited because the torso angle shifts forward at the bottom of a squat, which holds at the top don't train; the same applies to box squats in front squat position.
Some forward lean and hip hinge in a squat is fine as long as it isn't exaggerated.
Front rack holds help the setup and unrack and reduce the mental pressure of holding a front-racked bar, letting you rep more weight.
The front squat is an amazing leg and quad builder, which is why NH does it.
Front rack holds don't train the legs; they train the core and upper back statically for rigidity and stability.
NH's theory: thoracic extension correlates directly with the ability to keep the lumbar spine from rounding; he has never seen a strong extended thoracic spine with a rounded lower back.
Training thoracic extension gives a tighter setup on pulls from the floor, preventing injury and energy leaks and targeting the right muscles.
Isometric holds with supramaximal weight aren't very taxing on muscles or CNS since there's no range of motion, but they are mentally stressful, like a cold shower: fear without real danger.
Always do front rack holds inside the rack above the hooks; unrack, hold, re-rack, never walk the weight out (even Olympic lifters don't).
Set the pins so unracking needs minimal knee bend; deeper knee flexion turns it into a half squat and stresses the knees.
Start front rack holds with your front squat weight (e.g. two plates), then add 5, 10, 15, 20 lb week to week so the knees adapt and technique is mastered; progress comes fast.
NH holds five plates and calls himself a weakling; Olympic lifters weighing about 170 lb easily hold 700 lb.
NH avoids adding knee flexion during holds because his knees don't like it; watch knee stress even without range of motion.
Do front rack holds for time, not reps; NH does 4 sets of about 3-5 seconds, and sees no point going beyond 10 seconds.
The weight should feel like it is pushing your head down; you should feel it in the neck, as if your head will blow.
One warm-up set is enough if you already front squat; otherwise ramp up more slowly.
If the rack position fails mid-hold, reset rather than grind; stay vertical with elbows as high as possible.
Program front rack holds as a secondary lift, not strength work, and superset them (e.g. with RDLs or hip thrusts) since they need little rest. Doing them every 10-15 days still carries over.
